title: Prospective evaluation of quality of life and outcome of robot-assisted resection rectopexy for rectal prolapse
summary:
Background
In rectal prolapse, the last section of the intestine protrudes from its normal position and may become visible through the anus when straining or even permanently. This is often very distressing for those affected and can lead to involuntary bowel movements, constipation, pain, mucus or blood discharge, and a strong feeling of a foreign body. Many patients also report limitations in their everyday life, at work, and in their social life. Surgery is often the most effective treatment if symptoms persist or conservative measures do not provide sufficient relief.
A modern surgical method is robot-assisted resection rectopexy. In this procedure, the prolapsed intestine is returned to its correct position in the abdominal cavity and secured there. A section of the intestine is often removed to prevent excessive intestinal loops and improve symptoms such as constipation. Although this method is increasingly being used, there is currently only limited data on how patients' quality of life develops over a longer period of time after surgery.

Research question
This study investigates whether and to what extent the well-being and quality of life of patients improve after robot-assisted resection rectopexy. It also examines how symptoms such as constipation, involuntary bowel movements, and satisfaction with treatment change over time.

Methodology
This is an observational study conducted at a hospital. All participants will undergo the medically necessary surgery, regardless of the study. The study does not change the treatment, but only collects information about how patients feel before and after the surgery.
The plan is to include approximately 25 adult patients in the study over a period of two years. The prerequisite is that surgery is planned and the participants give their written consent.
Participation consists of completing questionnaires. These questionnaires assess general well-being, quality of life, and symptoms such as constipation or involuntary bowel movements. The questionnaires will be completed at three points in time: once before the surgery, then after six months, and again after twelve months. In addition, possible complications after the surgery, the length of the hospital stay, and the course of recovery will be documented.
All data will be treated confidentially and stored in such a way that it cannot be directly attributed to a specific person.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Indication for prolapse surgery for grade I-V rectal prolapse according to Oxford classification
Minimally invasive robotic surgery
Verbal and written consent
Ability to understand the content and scope of the study and to implement it
Exclusion criteria:
Incapacity to consent
Age < 18 years
Life expectancy < 12 months
